articles.title: Croatian supermarket prices from five chains
articles.excerpt: In an earlier article I described the Croatia Supermarket Prices Actor, which looks up prices by barcode from the price lists that chains publish on their own websites. Version 0.1.6 covers five chain…
articles.body: In an earlier article I described the Croatia Supermarket Prices Actor, which looks up prices by barcode from the price lists that chains publish on their own websites. Version 0.1.6 covers five chains: Lidl Hrvatska, Tommy, Metro Cash & Carry Hrvatska, KTC and Ribola. This post covers the 2026 price-list rule, how the Actor now handles empty store lists, the input, what the data does not have, and what a run costs. The 2026 price-list rule Croatia's rule on publishing price lists (Pravilnik o načinu objave cjenika proizvoda, NN 132/2026) has been in force since 17 November 2026. The README says it requires traders to publish price lists and to allow automated collection tools. It does not cover re-use.

articles.title: How We Stopped Playing Detective After Every Deployment: Fixing Release Audit Trails in CI/CD
articles.excerpt: Every developer loves a pipeline that ships from pull request to production in ten minutes—right up until something breaks at 3:00 AM or a security auditor asks for proof of what changed last Tuesday.…
articles.body: Every developer loves a pipeline that ships from pull request to production in ten minutes—right up until something breaks at 3:00 AM or a security auditor asks for proof of what changed last Tuesday. Suddenly, nobody can point to a single source of truth. Instead, three people end up playing detective across Slack threads, Git commit logs, Jira tickets, expired CI job outputs, and kubectl describe commands just to figure out which image digest is actually serving traffic. Shipping fast is a solved problem for most cloud-native teams. Keeping a trustworthy software release audit trail without burying developers in manual paperwork is where things fall apart.
articles.author: Sneha kumari

articles.title: Spring AI Explained: Build Your First AI Application with Spring Boot
articles.excerpt: Imagine you are building a Spring Boot application. You already know how to create REST APIs, connect to databases, implement business logic, and handle requests. Now imagine adding one more feature:…
articles.body: Imagine you are building a Spring Boot application. You already know how to create REST APIs, connect to databases, implement business logic, and handle requests. Now imagine adding one more feature: A user sends a question to your application, and your application generates an intelligent response using an AI model. For example: User: Explain Java interfaces with an example. AI: An interface in Java is a contract that defines methods a class must implement... How would you implement this? You could directly call an AI provider's REST API using Java's HTTP client. But then you would need to manage API requests, authentication, request formats, response parsing, and provider-specific details yourself. This is where Spring AI comes in.
articles.author: Mayur Bodhare

articles.title: Spec-Driven Development: How to Build Better Software With AI Coding Agents
articles.excerpt: AI coding tools have made it easier than ever to turn an idea into working software. A founder can describe a feature in natural language, generate a prototype, and see an application take shape withi…
articles.body: AI coding tools have made it easier than ever to turn an idea into working software. A founder can describe a feature in natural language, generate a prototype, and see an application take shape within hours. But there is a growing difference between generating code quickly and building software that actually meets business requirements. AI coding agents can produce impressive results when they understand the task. However, vague instructions, incomplete business rules, missing edge cases, and unclear acceptance criteria can lead to software that looks finished but behaves incorrectly. For businesses building SaaS products, MVPs, and custom applications, the solution is not necessarily a better AI model. It may be a better development process.
articles.author: Ubaid Ur Rahman

articles.title: The base_url Is the Whole Integration: LangChain Through a Gateway
articles.excerpt: Every LangChain app has a connection point, and it's smaller than you think. It's the ChatOpenAI constructor. Model name, key, done — that object decides which provider takes every call your chain mak…
articles.body: Every LangChain app has a connection point, and it's smaller than you think. It's the ChatOpenAI constructor. Model name, key, done — that object decides which provider takes every call your chain makes, what a retry looks like, and what evidence exists afterwards. ChatOpenAI takes a base_url. Point it at a gateway — here, nRouter at https://api.nrouter.ai/v1 — with a virtual key, and the chain's traffic runs through the gateway. Here's the part that matters: nothing else changes. from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI llm = ChatOpenAI ( model = "nrouter/auto" , api_key = "sk-nrouter-..." , base_url = "https://api.nrouter.ai/v1" , temperature = 0.2 , timeout = 60 , max_retries = 2 , model_kwargs = { "nrouter_cache" : True } , ) Prompt templates: unchanged. Memory: unchanged.

articles.title: All my tests passed. Then I sent 4 AI "users" into my app and they found 5 bugs
articles.excerpt: TL;DR "Harness" means everything around an AI model that isn't the model: sandbox, tools, instructions, tests. On the user side, harness engineering means making sure your agent never makes the same m…
articles.body: TL;DR "Harness" means everything around an AI model that isn't the model: sandbox, tools, instructions, tests. On the user side, harness engineering means making sure your agent never makes the same mistake twice. The easiest place to start: have AI play users with different habits and let them poke at your app. All my tests passed. They still found 5 bugs. Before fixing a bug, write a test that fails because of it. That's the step that actually "trains the harness." "Harness engineering" didn't click for me at first The term is everywhere right now. I read a few explainers ("designing the environment, constraints and feedback around an AI") and nodded along without really getting it.

articles.body: The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon)..

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 25, 1970: NASA's 'wingless' M2-F3 'lifting body' aircraft makes its 1st powered flight ahead of supersonic tests
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft. After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights. The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet.

articles.title: SpaceX Starship debris becomes art in Ashley Zelinskie's 'The Weight of Space' (video, photos)
articles.excerpt: Explore Ashley Zelinskie's 'The Weight of Space' Monuments in marble, Ejecta prints, Launch Sequence sculptures and interactive Crowded Sky at Heft Gallery in New York City.
articles.body: When a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan. 2025, pieces of its heat shield washed ashore. Some of that material now hangs on a gallery wall in New York City, embedded in artist Ashley Zelinskie's print of the very explosion it survived. Look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface. Some of Zelinskie's friends vacationing on the islands had come across pieces of heat-shield tile. "I think you might want these," Zelinskie recalled one friend telling her. She did. The Brooklyn-based artist ground the fragments into dust and worked them into the print. Ashley Zelinskie incorporated dust from recovered SpaceX Starship heat-shield tiles into this print of the vehicle breaking apart over Turks and Caicos.

articles.body: Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years. The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit. "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval. AI has become central to SpaceX's business plans and identity over the past year or so. For example, the company has said that it's eyeing a "total addressable market" of $28.5 trillion over the long haul — and nearly $23 trillion of that is in "enterprise AI applications." Starmind is key to those lofty ambitions.
